title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days, after studying all five domains and taking at least one mock. The aim is to sharpen what you know, not learn new material. Most days take an hour; the mock day about 2 hours, the next day up to 90 minutes.
how_it_works: Short reviews spread over several days hold up better than one long session the night before.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.
The real exam has no going back, so this week trains one careful read and a firm choice on each question.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with today's plan. Doubling up turns review into cramming.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the time of day your exam starts, to test your pace and focus.

tasks.text: Take a full timed mock in one sitting at your exam's start time. Block about 2 hours, turn notifications off and keep notes closed.
Practice the real exam's rhythm: about 55 seconds a question, answer each one once and never go back, even if the mock lets you.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: One mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. KaiSip's mock does not adapt like the real exam, so its score is only a rough guide.

days.title: Learn from every miss
days.goal: Trace each mock miss back to the thinking slip behind it. Stop after about 90 minutes, even if some are left.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from yesterday's mock, starting with Domains 1 and 4, the two heaviest.
Tag each miss: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy” (a skipped step), “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list three Domain 1 and three Domain 4 points. Then open the lists and check.
Read the principles on your role. “Acted as the wrong person” covers doing the owner’s job and passing up your own.

days.remember: “Missed FIRST or BEST” covers any priority word. Picked the close second? Tag the reason it lost.

days.title: Your biggest gap
days.goal: Work on your weakest domain. KaiSip picks it for you: a low score in a big domain counts most.

tasks.text: Before opening your focus domain's list, write down what you remember. Then check for gaps.
Answer a short set in that domain, rating how sure you are before you check each answer.
Review first the answers you felt sure of but got wrong. Those are the ones to fix.
For a topic you missed more than once, read its note, then close it and explain the idea in two sentences.
Read the principles on choosing the basic control that fits the risk.

days.remember: Weight matters: Domains 1 and 4 together carry about 45% of the exam.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your exam pace steady with one timed mini mock, and refresh who decides what.

tasks.text: Take a timed mini mock in one sitting. Answer each question once and move on; watch your pace more than the score.
From memory, list three Domain 2 and three Domain 3 points. Then open the lists and check.
Without looking, say who may accept a risk within tolerance and who decides beyond it. Then check the note.
Read the principles on what to protect first: people, then the goal at stake.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here on, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Read like the exam
days.goal: Sharpen how you read each question, work on your second gap and recall Domain 5.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Domain 5 points. Then open the list and check.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short set in your second-weakest domain. Name the priority word before you read the options.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: Several options are often true. The priority word and your role decide which one wins.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Recall everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details, so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each domain, recall two points before you open its list. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Read the principles on what to do when something goes wrong: report it, contain it and preserve evidence.
Read the ethics principles: due care, due diligence and the four canons weighed together.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels unclear.
Confirm your booking, your ID (both IDs if you are 18 or over) and your route, and reread the exam-day rules from ISC2 and your booking confirmation.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: answer up to 10 mistake journal questions, then stop. A miss today is a reminder, not a warning.
Read the reminder for the slip you make most often.
Read your pace plan once, then put it away.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and the work of preparing is already done.

eve: Your booking is confirmed, and you have checked the ID and exam-day rules from ISC2 and your booking confirmation.
Your route and travel time to the Pearson VUE test center are planned, with time to spare for check-in.
Aged 18 or over? Both IDs are laid out: a primary with photo and signature, a secondary with signature, both unexpired originals matching your booking name.
Aged 16 or 17? Your photo ID with your name is ready (a school ID works). Your parent or guardian brings a government photo-and-signature ID and signs the log sheet.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your pace plan: about 55 seconds a question, question 65 at the 1-hour mark and question 100 by about 92 minutes.
Leave early enough to reach the test center at least 30 minutes before your start time, as ISC2 asks. Arriving late can cost you your seat and your fee.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, reread the last line of the question, choose your best answer and move on.
Expect many questions to feel hard. An adaptive exam is built that way, so it says nothing about how you are doing.

points.text: Name the goal at stake: confidentiality (who can see it), integrity (is it still correct) or availability (can people use it). Personal data also raises privacy: should it be kept at all? Then match the control to the goal.

Identification claims who you are, authentication proves it, authorization sets what you may do and accounting records what you did. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) needs two different types: something you know, have or are.

Risk is likelihood and impact together. You rarely control the threat, so you lower risk by reducing weaknesses (likelihood) or limiting the damage (impact). Treatment options: avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept.
You never accept risk yourself. The risk owner accepts within tolerance, and senior management decides beyond it. Your job is to record the risk and route it to its owner.
Policies, standards and procedures are mandatory; guidelines only advise. A request to bypass policy goes through the exception process, whoever asks.

Controls are technical, administrative or physical, and each prevents, detects, corrects, deters, recovers or compensates. Prefer stopping harm first, and never let a lock trap people: escape-route doors must let people out and fail safe (unlock) without power.
Due diligence is finding out: research, assess, verify. Due care is acting on it: implement, enforce, fix. Know the four canons; in a dilemma, weigh them together, not by list order.

Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) means security follows the business's goals and rules. Your part: follow the policies, know who owns each system, and raise risks to that owner. Leaders can hand out tasks, but they stay accountable.
Disaster recovery restores IT. It is one part of business continuity, which also covers people, places, suppliers and communication. People's safety comes before any asset.

Business impact analysis (BIA) comes first. Recovery time objective (RTO): how fast a system must be back, inside the maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), the longest outage the business can bear. Recovery point objective (RPO): how much data you can lose.
Redundancy keeps service running when a part fails; backups bring back deleted, corrupted or encrypted data. A backup counts only when a restore has been tested and attackers can't reach it.

Plan tests run from least to most disruptive: checklist (read it), tabletop (talk it through), simulation (act it out), parallel (run the backup site alongside live), full interruption (switch live off). Choose the least disruptive test that meets the goal.
Urgency, authority and secrecy are warning signs. Verify through a channel you already trust, never one the requester supplies, and report every attempt, including your own click.

Key performance indicators (KPIs) show how well things run; key risk indicators (KRIs) warn that risk is rising. If a metric crosses its threshold, report it at once. Never change the number or the threshold yourself; only its owner can.
No ticket, no access. The owner approves, someone else sets it up, and the record shows both. Urgency changes how fast a request moves, never whether it is checked.

Joiners start with the smallest fitting role. Movers lose old access at the move, which stops privilege creep; only approved, time-limited handover access may stay. Leavers lose access the same day, and at once for a hostile exit.
In an access review, the owner confirms who should keep each access. Your part: remove what the owner says to remove, and record it. Access nobody confirms is removed.
Least privilege: only the access the task needs, for only as long as needed. Separation of duties: no one person can start, approve and hide a sensitive action.

Who decides access? The owner: discretionary (DAC). Labels the system enforces: mandatory (MAC). The job: role-based (RBAC). Several conditions at once: attribute-based (ABAC). One fixed rule for all: rule-based.
The more power an account has, the tighter its controls: a named account, phishing-resistant sign-in such as passkeys, a vault, time limits and recorded sessions.
Bots, service accounts and AI agents are identities too. Each needs an owner, a purpose, least privilege, logging and an end date.

Name the layer before the fix: a control protects only its own layer. Switches use MAC addresses (a device's hardware address) inside a network; routers use IP addresses between networks. Not the same MAC as mandatory access control.
Turn off services nobody needs, then use the encrypted version for the rest: SSH instead of Telnet for remote login, SFTP instead of FTP for file transfer, HTTPS instead of HTTP for websites.

Firewalls allow only what the business needs and deny the rest, with rule changes through change management. An intrusion detection system (IDS) alerts; an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and blocks.

Wi-Fi: use WPA3, the current standard, never the broken WEP. Treat IoT (internet-connected) devices as untrusted: inventory them, change defaults, segment them. With industrial control systems, protect people first and never scan or patch a live controller without approval.
Segment by trust: public-facing systems in the screened subnet (DMZ), guests and IoT on their own segments, sensitive data deeper inside. Micro-segmentation limits movement within a segment.
Defense in depth layers independent controls so one failure doesn't open everything. Zero Trust: verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach. Being inside the network earns no trust.

Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what it puts there, such as data, identities, access and settings, in IaaS (rented servers), PaaS (a platform to run your code) and SaaS (ready-made apps).
The data owner sets the classification; everyone else applies it. Protect unlabeled data at the higher level until the owner answers, and follow the label wherever the data goes.

Deleting is not sanitizing. Clear (overwrite so normal tools can't recover it) for low-risk reuse, purge (wipe so even lab tools can't) before sensitive media leaves your control, and destroy when it can't be purged. Verify, and keep the record.

Symmetric encryption suits bulk data; asymmetric exchanges keys and proves identity. A hash shows whether data changed; a digital signature shows who sent it and that it is unchanged. Neither keeps it secret.
Not every event is an incident. Triage by impact, not arrival order, and hand anything over the threshold to the incident response team instead of carrying on alone.
Incident order: contain, then eradicate, then recover, then lessons learned. Isolate rather than power off unless the playbook says otherwise, and restore only from clean sources.
Preserve first, analyze later, and only within your role. Don't browse, copy or clean a suspect device; write down what you saw and did, and record every handoff.
No change without approval, testing and a way back; urgency speeds approval but never skips it. Security testing needs the owner's written authorization and a clear scope.

principles.intro: The CC mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. What must happen before anything else? If people are in danger, their safety comes first. Otherwise, follow the procedure's order, and report what is outside your role before acting alone.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what does everything else depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the one that best fits the facts: it stays within your role, follows policy and fits the risk. A basic control that fits beats an advanced one that doesn't.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which fits my role, the policy and the risk?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST effective or MOST important. Judge every option on that quality alone.
The main purpose or reason, not a side benefit or a nice extra.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what is this mainly for?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For risk or concern, the worst harm, with harm to people weighing heaviest; for benefit, the strongest gain.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and for whom?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. Which outcome is most probable from the facts given, even if another would be worse?
Flip the logic. Three options do the job; find the one that does it worst or not at all.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is being asked: an action, a risk, a purpose or a definition.

answering_routine.title: Find the priority word
answering_routine.text: Find the priority word (FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST) and keep it in mind while you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Check your role and the stakes
answering_routine.text: You are an entry-level practitioner unless told otherwise. Are people at risk? Is this yours to do, or the owner's to decide?

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Wrong control type, wrong layer, outside your authority, a skipped procedure or a fix for a symptom.

answering_routine.title: Decide between the final two
answering_routine.text: Apply the priority word, then prefer the option that keeps people safe, follows the procedure, fits your role and fixes the cause.

answering_routine.title: Commit and move on
answering_routine.text: Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice, then confirm. You can't come back to it.

pace: Up to 125 questions in 2 hours is a little under a minute each. Aim for about 55 seconds so even the longest exam fits.
Checkpoints: question 65 at the 1-hour mark, question 100 by about 92 minutes. Ahead is fine; keep the same care.
The exam is adaptive: once you finalize an answer, you can't go back to review or change it. Give each question one careful read, then commit.
Past about 90 seconds on one question, eliminate what you can, choose your best answer and move on.
Make sure you reach at least question 100 within the 2 hours. Running out of time before that is an automatic fail.
The exam can stop anywhere from question 100 to 125; where it stops tells you nothing. Trial questions look like the rest, so treat each question as if it counts.
